passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: The admissible harmonic lattice is an arithmetic restriction on the entire perturbation. For azimuthal order $m\geq1$, the label map is injective, respects reflection and negation, and has image exactly the integer pairs $(\nu,k)$ with $m\mid k$ and $\nu+k/m$ even. Combining that arithmetic with the mode exclusion interface makes every off-lattice velocity, gradient, and second derivative coefficient vanish almost everywhere in space-time. The support conclusion therefore applies to the derivative data used by the cell calculus, as well as to the velocity.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: Real tensor fields have conjugate coefficients at opposite harmonic labels. A separate transformation law describes what happens under a time shift $s$ and axial rotation $\phi$: each coefficient acquires the phase $e^{i(2\pi\nu s+k\phi)}$, while the gradient has two rotated indices and the second derivative has three. The conjugacy identity is stated for arbitrary real input fields. The shift and rotation identities require time periodicity and integrability of the relevant orbit functions; these hypotheses justify moving the transformations through the mode averages.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: Rotation averaging preserves the spatial integral of any almost everywhere measurable nonnegative extended-valued function. The normalization is $1/(2\pi)$, with the angular integral over $[0,2\pi]$. The source uses preservation of volume by axial rotations and interchange of nonnegative integrals. Since the statement is an equality of extended integrals, it remains meaningful before finiteness has been established; it does not supply finiteness of an energy by itself.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: Temporal cosine and sine components retain the local second order field structure. When the parity condition $n+\nu$ even holds, their spatial modes combine into the complex velocity, gradient, and second derivative profiles used by the cell machinery. These identities hold for almost every meridian point with positive radius. The pressure companion establishes the corresponding velocity-style profile identity for a periodic pressure field. It supplies the pressure component of the representation without asserting the full perturbation equations or replacing the periodic pressure assumption.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: Integrability near the axis comes in two different forms. A local second order field gives ordinary integrability of its velocity and gradient modes on meridian strips that include radius zero. For a periodic perturbation, the axis interface gives integrability of radius times each velocity, gradient, and second derivative component. The radial factor matters: the latter statement alone does not remove the cylindrical weight from a Hessian component. The source proves these facts through bounded mode kernels and local integrability, with a cutoff argument for the unweighted gradient modes.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: The second derivative energy identity equates the period integral of the squared Frobenius norm of the Hessian with that of the squared norm of its trace. The perturbation supplies weak first and second derivatives and finite gradient energy. The source first obtains the spatial identity for almost every time slice and then integrates those equalities over the period. This is an identity of nonnegative extended integrals, so any later claim that both sides are finite needs its own finiteness hypothesis.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: The scalar mode interface transports a weak spatial gradient into a weak derivative in height. Under joint measurability, local period-integrated square bounds, periodicity, and the stated reflection hypothesis, the scalar plane mode has the advertised height derivative on every interval $(-h,h)$ for almost every positive radius. The source uses a countable dense collection of one-dimensional test functions to choose one exceptional radial null set. Consequently, the same good radii work for all positive heights, rather than a separately chosen set for each interval.

anchor.heading: 1. From real fields to harmonic data

passages.section: 1. From real fields to harmonic data
passages.quote: Compact support of the given shape is controlled by the compactified chart. Valid shape parameters, compact time-field data, and the edge-break condition force the assembled physical field to vanish whenever the spatial radius exceeds $\text{chartLength}\,t_b/(1-t_b)$. The proof shows that every finite key contribution is zero beyond that edge and then sums the contributions. The radius bound concerns this explicitly assembled field; it is not a general support theorem for arbitrary perturbations.

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: The upper and lower plane traces are integral functionals of a function and its weak height derivative. Reflection exchanges them, with the derivative changing sign. If the pair satisfies the weak derivative relation on a larger interval, the upper and lower traces agree, and the upper trace is independent of the positive height used in its integral formula. The source proves matching with smooth approximations to a tent test and dominated convergence; height independence is proved through a weak primitive representative. These results justify a common plane trace without assuming an arbitrary representative has a prescribed point value.

anchor.heading: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: A side trace at a fixed coordinate is independent of the auxiliary coordinate used to define its averaging interval. Both auxiliary coordinates and the trace coordinate must lie strictly inside a common interval on which the weak derivative relation holds, and neither auxiliary coordinate may equal the trace coordinate. The source compares the resulting tent identities in all relative-order cases. This is the compatibility fact that permits adjacent constructions to use different strip widths while referring to the same weak trace.

anchor.heading: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: Height strip moments can be evaluated as radial integrals of one-dimensional trace functionals. The general formula allows distinct height coordinates and continuous radial weights, assuming weighted integrability of both the field and its height derivative. The specialization with endpoints zero and a positive height identifies the cell formula's strip moment with the upper plane trace. The orientation signs and affine height weights are part of these identities; they are not discarded by interpreting the strip as an informal boundary integral.

anchor.heading: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: Corner data are also integrated trace functionals. The reflection identity reverses the height coordinate, changes the signs of the vertical and mixed derivatives, and carries along any complex scalar factor. The matching theorem identifies the positive-height and negative-height corner moments under weak plane derivative assumptions on a larger rectangle. The trace formula then expresses a corner moment as a radial integral of upper traces of the field and radial derivative, with explicit orientation and affine radial weights. None of these declarations introduces point evaluation at an arbitrary corner representative.

anchor.heading: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: At the reflection plane, velocity strip and corner data inherit the component sign of the reflected mode, while the vertical-gradient strip data gain an additional minus sign. Their integration heights may be different on the two sides. The velocity strip identity permits radial intervals reaching the axis; the gradient identity additionally requires an axis-admissible test, which supplies the needed radial factor when the interval starts at zero. The corner identity permits an auxiliary radial endpoint at zero while keeping the corner radius positive and the two radii distinct. These statements combine weak traces, mode reflection, and axis integrability under an actual reflection symmetry of the perturbation.

anchor.heading: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives

passages.section: 2. Traces without pointwise representatives
passages.quote: Harmonic side data agree exactly with the segment moment formulas used by the cell layout. Velocity data use the velocity profile together with its radial and height derivatives. Gradient data select the radial or height derivative according to the segment orientation and use the corresponding second derivative profiles. The harmonic layout, periodic field structure, pressure interface, and parity condition are explicit inputs. This correspondence is what lets finite side-data coordinates represent weak field moments without requiring pointwise boundary samples.

passages.section: 3. Turning plane traces into quantitative credit
passages.quote: A patch trace obeys a weighted energy estimate on an annular meridian rectangle away from the axis. The squared trace norm is bounded by the product of the reflected velocity energy weighted by a positive charge $b$ and a test-gradient energy weighted by $1/b$, both with cylindrical radial measure. The test is Lipschitz, vanishes on the two radial sides and top, and the charge has positive lower and finite upper bounds. Its gradient energy includes the azimuthal frequency term. Reflection and weak-height-trace interfaces supply the integration identity before the Cauchy-type bound is applied.

anchor.heading: 3. Turning plane traces into quantitative credit

passages.section: 3. Turning plane traces into quantitative credit
passages.quote: The inverse-Gram step converts all scalar testing inequalities into one vector credit. If a positive definite real matrix $G$ bounds $|c^*t|^2$ by $A\,c^*Gc$ for every complex coefficient vector, with $A\geq0$, then the inverse quadratic form of $t$ is at most $A$. Applied to finite combinations of patch tests, this turns the trace energy estimate into an inverse-Gram bound on their collected traces. The matrix is required to dominate the test-gradient energy for every complex combination, not merely for each test separately.

passages.section: 3. Turning plane traces into quantitative credit
passages.quote: A valid credit patch packages those tests, their trace-data map, a positive definite test matrix, and a credit matrix dominated by its inverse form. The bridge proves that the credit quadratic form evaluated on the actual field data is bounded by the charge-weighted reflected velocity energy on the patch region. The proof first identifies the matrix trace-data vector with the analytical patch traces, then applies the inverse-Gram estimate. Validity of the supplied patch data and the perturbation's reflection symmetry remain hypotheses.

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: For a skeleton key whose spatial mode is zero, reversing the temporal frequency conjugates its field harmonic. At temporal frequency zero the same key harmonic has zero imaginary part. These statements apply to the key-layout functionals of the field, derivative, and pressure data. Their scope is deliberately restricted by the key-mode condition: they do not assert reality of arbitrary nonzero spatial-mode keys or impose a gauge condition on the field.

anchor.heading: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: A nonprivate local datum can be transported to a shared skeleton key in two stages. First, harmonic trace independence and valid cell layouts identify the local head functional with the corresponding key harmonic. Second, an admissible key evaluation transfers that harmonic to its canonical label and mode, including the specified conjugation and reflection operations. The transfer requires a key in the designated half-plane, the stated key-mode or stream-key condition, and the plane-flip interface. These hypotheses prevent an arbitrary coordinate identification from being mistaken for an analytic equality.

anchor.heading: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: Odd temporal stream keys vanish on the reflection plane at every nonnegative radial endpoint. The source combines cosine and sine strip moments, applies the reflected vertical-component sign, and obtains an equality with its own negative; the zero-length case is handled separately. The theorem assumes the plane-trace facts, the field hypotheses, and agreement between the key layout's order and the layer's azimuthal order. It is a specific stream-key identity on the plane, not a statement that the whole odd-frequency field vanishes.

anchor.heading: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: The zero-spatial-mode velocity keys satisfy flux identities in terms of stream-key differences. On a radial side with positive level, the velocity moment is a scaled difference of endpoint stream values. On a height side, the zeroth velocity moment is reconstructed from the first moment and the endpoint stream difference, with a nonzero test coefficient required for division. The provider derives both identities for each real cosine or sine tuple using the local second order field obtained from harmonic lifting.

anchor.heading: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: The normal-segment identity expresses a normal gradient moment using velocity moments and corner data. On radial segments it includes the reciprocal radius and the azimuthal coupling; on height segments the corner terms carry radial endpoint weights. The polynomial derivative of the chosen test must be representable in the supplied test basis, and the segment endpoints must match the declared corners. Harmonic lifting proves the real cosine and sine identities and then combines them into the complex data identity. This is the analytic content used by normal rows.

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: Row matching is proved by row kind with an explicit induction premise. A row may use already matched, nonunused rows of strictly smaller rank. Key rows use the local-to-shared identification and canonical evaluation; derived rows use the cell relations and the lower-rank data; normal rows use the normal-segment identity. The common row-kind contract concludes equality of the finite row value with the corresponding shifted field datum. Its rank condition makes the dependency direction visible and does not grant circular row identities.

passages.section: 4. Shared keys and finite row compatibility
passages.quote: Once every relevant row agrees with the actual periodic field data, the row identity transfers to the true state of an admissible tuple. The provider substitutes the chosen recovered pressure into the field-level statement, using its periodicity and reflection properties. The conclusion is equality for every row whose reason is not unused. Pressure recovery and chosen-pressure symmetry are therefore part of the bridge from field equations to matrix state coordinates, rather than consequences of an arbitrary row matrix.

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: Weak admissibility is assembled from two explicit collections of clauses. The weight collection supplies positivity, regularity, decay, axisymmetry, and the auxiliary convolution and share conditions. The remaining collection supplies period and weight bounds, harmonic expansion and amplitude bounds, one-sided frame-frequency controls, global share bounds, and the comparison with the convolution allowance. The provider fills the corresponding weak-admissibility record field by field. It combines established obligations; it does not infer those bounds from the existence of numerical arrays.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: The regularity of the true field used by assembly consists of cell-profile regularity and measurability of cell densities, stretching integrands, given modes, and exterior densities. The provider obtains this package from the field-regularity record, which already contains a valid mesh, a positive azimuthal order, a weak model state, harmonic and symmetry information, admissibility, measurable bound data, and actuator shape facts. This is the bridge that makes later integrals legitimate for the actual perturbation data.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: The cell allocation identity is preceded by a precise finiteness result: the negative cell part and both positive and negative off-cell parts are finite for every admissible cell tuple. Its assumptions include finite negative form, coefficient lower bounds, the shared coercivity coefficient, valid cell calculus, and regular charges. The allocation split then rewrites the real-valued cell contribution minus its off-cell contribution as the sum of resolved energy, off-charge contribution, and stretching. The finiteness contract does not itself assert finiteness of the positive cell part, so that stronger assertion should not be read into the conversion to real-valued expressions.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: The stretching contribution first becomes a quadratic harmonic pairing of the true velocity and gradient profiles. A second identity splits that pairing into the upper-profile self-term, three cross interactions with the resolved remainder, the band, and the deactivated modes, and the other-profile self-term. Each cross term has its factor of two. The expansion uses the mode-class and regularity data; the finer split also assumes the low-tail decomposition. This exact bookkeeping identifies which later bounds must pay for each interaction.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: The leaf comparison bounds the true leaf pairing plus the box contribution, after subtracting the retained low-profile leaf pairing, by resolved energy minus the energy budget and tail credit. It is an inequality for every allowed choice of cell pins and ports. The provider needs finite cell pieces and valid cell calculus in addition to field regularity. This is where the finite leaf representation is compared with the field energy while retaining the unresolved contribution as an explicit budget.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: Absorption loss has two exact decompositions. The other-profile absorption equals the absorption of the low-band state plus that of the actual tail profiles. The latter is a finite sum over resolved labels of curl, strain, and velocity tail squares multiplied by the corresponding leaf absorption coefficients. The first equality uses the low-tail split; the second uses the valid mesh and cell calculus. Together they identify the coefficients that must appear in the later tail budget, rather than merely bounding an unspecified remainder.

anchor.heading: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities

passages.section: 5. Finiteness and allocation before inequalities
passages.quote: The sharp-bound regularity package justifies the infinite harmonic operations locally. It gives almost everywhere summability of the squared other-profile norms and of the charge and stretching terms; the summed charge and stretching terms are integrable. It identifies the integrals of those two sums with the named charge amount and true stretching pairing, and supplies integrability of the resolved leaf, box, and absorption cores. These conclusions are conditional on the regularity, potential, and low-tail interfaces and are localized to each cell rectangle.

passages.section: 6. Paying for the potential interactions
passages.quote: The long harmonic model estimate separates frequency bands on the time-angle torus. It assumes integrable matrix coefficients, operator bounds on the symmetric stretching matrix and the gradient matrix, and vanishing low Fourier coefficients of the model matrix through the specified cutoff. The conclusion bounds the resolved self-pairing plus twice the resolved-tail pairing from below by the negative of the summed quadratic charges. The charge weights distinguish the low band from its complement through the chosen positive splitting parameter. This is a finite harmonic matrix estimate with torus facts as inputs, not the entire cell coercivity statement.

anchor.heading: 6. Paying for the potential interactions

passages.section: 6. Paying for the potential interactions
passages.quote: The two tail estimates pay for different interactions. The resolved-tail cross estimate puts the negative port quadratic form minus the strain and velocity balance costs below twice the model and leaf cross pairings. The high-partner estimate bounds the high-frequency partner charge of the actual tails by explicit strain and velocity tail costs, including the radius bound and the positive Young parameters. The cross estimate uses the low-tail split; the high-partner estimate has its own structural hypotheses. Their separate conclusions explain why both kinds of tail charges remain visible in the potential budget.

anchor.heading: 6. Paying for the potential interactions

passages.section: 6. Paying for the potential interactions
passages.quote: The charge stage compares the available charge surplus with a specific sum of demands: band energy, row and pairing leakage, group and partner charges, band allowances, credits, and pairing slack on the band and designated deactivated labels. Its conclusion is that this entire sum is at most the surplus. The provider depends on the actual potential conditions and regular field data. It is the accounting inequality that allows many individually estimated interactions to draw on one charge allocation without dropping a cost.

anchor.heading: 6. Paying for the potential interactions

passages.section: 6. Paying for the potential interactions
passages.quote: Potential assembly combines the previously separated expansion, leaf, sharp, model, cross-tail, group, charge, high-tail, resolved-error, and split identities. The resulting inequality controls the retained potential quadratic form, the band quadratic and linear terms, leakage, allowances, credits, and slack, while subtracting the explicit resolved tail costs. Its right-hand side is resolved energy plus off-charge contribution plus stretching, minus the energy budget and tail credit. The assembly theorem is conditional on those component stages; its value is a correctly signed aggregate inequality, not a replacement for checking the component hypotheses.

anchor.heading: 6. Paying for the potential interactions

passages.section: 6. Paying for the potential interactions
passages.quote: The final tail stage uses a top-block estimate that bounds each velocity tail square by a finite quadratic form plus a strain tail square divided by the velocity-tail gain. Combined with the tail-absorption and gain interfaces, it bounds the negative top quadratic form by tail credit minus the total strain, velocity, and curl costs. Positivity and admissibility of the gains belong to the tail conditions. This is the precise point at which the remaining tail costs can be absorbed into the assembled cell inequality.

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: A conjugate-closed finite cell vector field is recovered from its harmonic labels in the rotating frame. For almost every meridian point in a valid cell rectangle, every time, angle, and component satisfies the finite Fourier reconstruction formula. The source derives the identity from the cylindrical representation and uses conjugacy to identify the real physical field with the complex reconstruction. The exceptional meridian null set remains in the statement, so the formula is not a claim of pointwise equality on every geometric seam.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The exact row decomposition starts with the actual forcing moment and subtracts the retained row vector and tail row. The remainder is the sum of frequency, model error, long interaction, deactivated-mode, and actuator pieces. The provider uses finite actuator harmonic support, cell-state membership, and the regularity and row-functional conditions. This identity identifies the quantities that must be estimated before a finite row norm can be charged to physical forcing and error allowances.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The frequency and long-interaction pieces are estimated in their designated inverse weighted row norms. The frequency norm is controlled by the frequency allowance. The long-interaction norm is controlled by the sum of long allowances over the resolved labels, band labels, and deactivated source labels. The scaling matrices and costs are those specified by the row conditions. Keeping the three long-interaction label sets explicit matters because they are assigned to different budget terms in the allowance split.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The deactivated row remainder is first written exactly as the sum of its group pieces. A separate estimate bounds the deactivation cost times the sum of the groups' inverse row-Gram norms by the deactivation allowance. The group identity uses the potential and row-functional conditions; the norm estimate uses the row and potential conditions governing the costs and groups. These are distinct steps: the identity organizes the unresolved modes, and the inequality pays for the organized sum.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The actuator contribution is bounded in the inverse norm associated with its scaled row Gram matrix. The right-hand side is the product of the actuator cost, the certified actuator error coefficient, and the sum of squares of the actuator coordinates. The provider requires the cell-state, field-regularity, row, and row-functional interfaces. Thus the coordinate error appears as an explicit quadratic cost, rather than being silently identified with an exact actuator expansion.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The allowance split directs the row errors to their available resources. Frequency, resolved model error, resolved long interaction, and resolved pairing slack fit inside the box amount. Band model error and band long interaction fit inside the band allowance. The corresponding deactivated-source terms, together with the deactivation allowance, fit inside row leakage. These three inequalities are the bridge from local error estimates to the specific budget terms that are available in the potential assembly.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: Combining the exact row decomposition with the frequency, model-error, long-interaction, deactivation, actuator, and allowance bounds yields the row moment inequality. It controls the inverse leak-Gram norm of the forcing moment minus the retained and tail rows, together with resolved pairing slack, by leakage, box and band allowances, and the actuator-coordinate cost. The companion provider packages these component interfaces into a reusable row-moment statement. The model-error estimate is an explicit input alongside the providers discussed here; no missing estimate is supplied merely by naming the assembled statement.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The forcing share agrees with the inverse base-row-weight norm of the stacked forcing moments. Row removal then compares the retained-row norm with that norm of forcing moments, the resolved strain and velocity tail costs, and the inverse leak-Gram norm of the remaining row mismatch. This is the quantitative step that permits retained coefficients to be removed from the final right-hand side. It preserves the mismatch term until the row moment estimate has paid for it.

anchor.heading: 7. The forcing row budget

passages.section: 7. The forcing row budget
passages.quote: The row stage combines stacked forcing-share equality, row removal, and the row moment inequality. Its conclusion bounds the retained-row norm plus resolved pairing slack by the actual forcing share, resolved strain and velocity tail costs, row leakage, the box and band allowances, and the actuator-coordinate cost. The provider assumes the row values, row conditions, field regularity, and band-profile integrability needed to use those pieces. It gives the forcing contribution in the form required by the cell assembly while keeping every remaining tail and error charge explicit.
